mechanism: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive: true positives divided by all people who truly have disease.
vignette: A new screening test is evaluated in 100 people who are known by a reference standard to have a disease. The screening test is positive in 90 of them and negative in 10.
lead: What is the sensitivity of the screening test?
distractors: Cannot be calculated without knowing disease prevalence
distractor_notes: 10% is the false-negative proportion in this group, not sensitivity.
50% does not follow from the true-positive and false-negative counts.
The denominator for sensitivity is all persons with disease, 90+10=100, not 110.
Sensitivity can be calculated from diseased subjects alone and does not require population prevalence.
key_expl: Sensitivity = true positives / (true positives + false negatives) = 90/(90+10) = 90%.
objective: Calculate and interpret sensitivity from a 2×2 diagnostic-test table.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A
sources.locator: Figure 5.10: Predictive Value Positive, Sensitivity, and Specificity
sources.support: CDC defines sensitivity as A/(A+C), the proportion of true cases detected by a test or surveillance system.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Glossary
sources.support: CDC defines sensitivity as the ability of a test or case definition to identify true cases.

mechanism: Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative: true negatives divided by all people who truly do not have disease.
vignette: A diagnostic test is evaluated in 200 people confirmed by a reference standard not to have the disease. The test is negative in 170 and positive in 30.
lead: What is the specificity of the test?
distractors: Cannot be calculated without knowing the number of diseased patients
distractor_notes: 15% is the false-positive proportion among disease-free subjects, not specificity.
70% is not derived from the stated true-negative and false-positive counts.
Specificity uses true negatives divided by all disease-free subjects: 170/(170+30), not 170/230.
Specificity can be calculated from the disease-free group without knowing how many diseased people were studied.
key_expl: Specificity = true negatives / (true negatives + false positives) = 170/(170+30) = 85%.
objective: Calculate specificity from disease-free subjects in a diagnostic-test validation study.
clues: 200 people truly do not have disease

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A
sources.support: CDC gives specificity as D/(B+D), the proportion of noncases correctly identified as negative.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Glossary
sources.support: CDC defines specificity as the ability of a test or case definition to exclude people without the health condition.

mechanism: For a test with unchanged sensitivity and specificity, positive predictive value decreases as disease prevalence falls because a larger fraction of positive results are false positives.
vignette: A screening test with fixed sensitivity and specificity is used first in a high-risk specialty clinic and then in a much lower-prevalence community population.
lead: Compared with use in the high-risk clinic, which test characteristic is expected to decrease in the community population?
distractors: Probability that a truly diseased patient tests positive
distractor_notes: Sensitivity is an intrinsic conditional performance measure and is assumed fixed in the scenario.
Specificity is also stipulated to remain fixed.
The analytic detection threshold is a laboratory property and does not change merely because population prevalence changes.
The probability that a diseased patient tests positive is sensitivity, which is specified as unchanged.
key_expl: Positive predictive value depends on disease prevalence; lower prevalence produces a lower proportion of true disease among all positive test results when sensitivity and specificity are unchanged.
objective: Predict the effect of disease prevalence on positive predictive value.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5 Quiz Answers
sources.support: CDC notes that predictive value positive is a function of both test/surveillance sensitivity and disease prevalence.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A
sources.support: CDC defines predictive value positive as the proportion of detected positive cases that truly have disease.

mechanism: Risk ratio compares cumulative incidence in an exposed group with cumulative incidence in an unexposed group.
vignette: In a cohort study, 40 of 200 exposed participants develop a disease during follow-up. Among 200 otherwise comparable unexposed participants, 10 develop the disease.
lead: What is the risk ratio for disease in exposed compared with unexposed participants?
distractor_notes: 0.25 reverses the comparison, corresponding to risk in unexposed divided by risk in exposed.
2.0 underestimates the ratio of 20% to 5%.
3.0 is not the quotient of the two incidence proportions.
8.0 doubles the correct risk ratio.
key_expl: Risk among exposed = 40/200 = 0.20; risk among unexposed = 10/200 = 0.05; RR = 0.20/0.05 = 4.0.
objective: Calculate a risk ratio from cohort incidence proportions.
clues: cohort design with exposed and unexposed groups

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 3, Section 5
sources.support: CDC defines risk ratio as risk in the group of interest divided by risk in the comparison group.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 3, Section 2
sources.support: CDC defines incidence proportion as new cases divided by the population at risk at the start of the period.

diagnosis: Odds ratio in a case-control study
mechanism: In a case-control study the exposure odds ratio is calculated by the cross-product ad/bc and is the standard measure of exposure-disease association because disease risks cannot usually be directly calculated.
vignette: A case-control study includes 100 patients with a disease and 100 controls. Among the cases, 60 had the exposure of interest and 40 did not. Among controls, 30 were exposed and 70 were unexposed.
lead: What is the odds ratio for the association between exposure and disease?
distractor_notes: 0.29 is approximately the inverse of the correct odds ratio.
1.5 reflects neither the cross-product ratio nor a valid risk calculation from these data.
2.0 is the ratio of exposed cases to exposed controls, not the odds ratio.
4.7 is not obtained from the 2×2 cross-product calculation.
objective: Calculate and interpret an odds ratio from a case-control 2×2 table.
clues: exposure counts given separately among cases and controls

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 3, Section 5
